draft.title: Social structure
card: Elite families
Old, wealthy families held land and the main local offices. They sat at the top of society in Pompeii and Herculaneum.
Freedmen
Former slaves who had been given their freedom by their owners. Some freedmen became rich through trade and could gain great influence.
Slaves
People owned by others, who worked in homes, shops, workshops and farms. They had few rights, but an owner could choose to free them.
Women
Women's status varied with their rank. Some wealthy women owned property or led in public life, while others, such as slaves, had little freedom.
draft.remember: Rank shaped life in the towns, but a freed slave could still rise to wealth and influence.

a.q: Which group in Pompeii was made up of former slaves who had been given their freedom?
opts: Freedmen
Elite families
Slaves
Women of high rank
a.why: Freedmen were slaves who had been freed by their owners. Slaves are the tempting wrong answer, because freedmen began as slaves, but slaves were still owned by others and had not been freed.
a.clue: Think of people who used to be slaves but no longer are.

b.q: Gaius, a freedman in Pompeii, runs a successful wine business and grows wealthy. What does his case best show about the town's society?
opts: Birth as a slave did not always block a rise to wealth
Freedmen were treated as equals of the elite families
All slaves in the town could expect to be freed
Only elite families were able to make money from trade
b.why: The card says some freedmen became rich and gained influence, so a slave's origin did not always limit them. The tempting wrong option is that freedmen were equal to elite families: wealth did not mean they held the same rank as old families.
b.clue: Wealth alone does not mean the same rank as the elite.

b.best: Birth as a slave did not always block a rise to wealth

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a qualifier ('did not always'). The three distractors are absolute claims ('Only', 'All', 'equals'), so a student could pick the answer by spotting the hedge without knowing the idea.

'Birth as a slave' is imprecise. The card defines freedmen as former slaves, and not all of them were born slaves (some were enslaved later, for example through war). Something like 'Having been a slave did not always block a rise to wealth' would match the card.
The question only restates the card's definition, and the clue ('people who used to be slaves but no longer are') repeats the question stem. This is very easy recall for Year 12 HSC.

proposal.title: Social structure
card: Elite families
Old, wealthy families owned land and filled the main local offices. They sat at the top of society in Pompeii and Herculaneum.
Freedmen
Former slaves freed by their owners. Some grew rich through trade, but they could not hold the main local offices, so many sought status as Augustales, priests of the emperor's cult.
Slaves
People owned by others, who worked in homes, shops, workshops and farms. They had few rights, but an owner could choose to free them.
Women
Women's status varied with their rank. Some wealthy women owned property or held public priesthoods, while others, such as slaves, had little freedom.
proposal.remember: Rank shaped life in the towns, but a freed slave could still rise to wealth and influence.

a.q: Why might a rich freedman in Pompeii seek to become one of the Augustales?
opts: He could not hold the main local offices
He needed the role to gain his freedom
The role made him one of the elite families
The role let him own property for the first time
a.why: Freedmen were barred from the main local offices, so becoming an Augustalis gave them public status another way. Becoming one of the elite families is tempting, but the role did not change a freedman's rank or make him part of the old families.
a.clue: Think about what a freedman's wealth still could not buy him.

b.q: Gaius, a freedman in Pompeii, runs a successful wine business and grows wealthy. What does his case best show about the town's society?
opts: Having been a slave did not always block a rise to wealth
Wealth usually let a freedman hold the top local offices
Slaves were often freed by the town council, not owners
Trade usually freed a slave without the owner's choice
b.why: Gaius was once a slave, yet he became rich through trade, so a slave past did not always stop a rise to wealth. The option about offices is tempting, but freedmen could not hold the main local offices, however rich they became.
b.clue: Separate what changed for Gaius from what stayed the same.

a.best: He could not hold the main local offices
